title: Ἐκ Κρήτης ἐς Θεσπρωτούς
titleEn: The Cretan’s Tale: Egypt, the Phoenician, the Wreck — Odyssey 14.199–320
part: The Cretan’s Tale: Egypt, the Phoenician, the Wreck (14.199–320)
about: Odysseus goes on with the account of himself that he began in the previous part. He says he is a Cretan, the son of a rich man by a bought concubine, who won wealth and standing by raiding overseas, and who was made to lead Cretan ships to Troy. After the war he stays at home one month and sails for Egypt with nine ships. His men plunder the Egyptian fields and are routed by the army that answers the alarm; he saves his own life by throwing down his arms and begging the king for mercy, and the king spares him; he stays seven years in Egypt, gathering gifts. A Phoenician then lures him to Phoenicia and puts him on a ship for Libya, meaning to sell him there. Zeus strikes the ship with lightning; Odysseus, holding the mast, is carried for nine days to the land of the Thesprotians, where their king’s son brings him to his father’s house.

sentences.t:
ἐκ μὲν Κρητάων γένος εὔχομαι εὐρειάων,
ἀνέρος ἀφνειοῖο πάϊς·
sentences.l:
From broad Crete my birth I declare,
of a rich man a son;
sentences.i: I declare my birth to be from broad Crete, a rich man’s son;
sentences.n: This part opens in the middle of the speech Odysseus began in the previous part: no quotation mark is opened here, and none is closed anywhere in this part, because he is still speaking at its last line. γένος εὔχομαι is ‘I declare my birth’: εὔχομαι is the house ‘declare’, here with an object (at 204 the same words take the infinitive εἶναι). Κρητάων … εὐρειάων is a plural, feminine as εὐρειάων shows, with the genitive ending -άων (Attic -ῶν); why Crete is plural is not clear, and both layers read it as the one island, as the singular Κρήτης does at 252. ἀνέρος is ἀνδρός, the genitive of ἀνήρ with its stem vowel kept, and ἀφνειοῖο ‘rich’ has -οιο for -ου; πάϊς ‘son’ is a nominative in apposition to the ‘I’ of εὔχομαι.

sentences.t:
πολλοὶ δὲ καὶ ἄλλοι
υἱέες ἐν μεγάρῳ ἠμὲν τράφεν ἠδ’ ἐγένοντο
γνήσιοι ἐξ ἀλόχου·
sentences.i: and many other sons besides were both brought up and born in the hall, the legitimate sons of his wife;
sentences.n: πολλοὶ δὲ καὶ ἄλλοι υἱέες is ‘and many other sons besides’: υἱέες is the uncontracted nominative plural (Attic υἱεῖς). ἠμὲν … ἠδ’ is ‘both … and’, joining τράφεν ‘were brought up’ and ἐγένοντο ‘were born’; τράφεν is the unaugmented aorist passive of τρέφω (= ἐτράφησαν). γνήσιοι is ‘legitimate’, in apposition to the sons, and ἐξ ἀλόχου ‘from a wife’ says why: ἄλοχος is plainly ‘wife’, and it is γνήσιοι that makes her the lawful one, set against the παλλακίς of the next unit. ἐν μεγάρῳ is ‘in the hall’, the rich man’s house.

sentences.t:
ἐμὲ δ’ ὠνητὴ τέκε μήτηρ
παλλακίς, ἀλλά με ἶσον ἰθαιγενέεσσιν ἐτίμα
Κάστωρ Ὑλακίδης,
sentences.l:
me but a bought mother bore,
a concubine, but me equally with the lawfully-born honoured
Castor, son of Hylax,
sentences.i: A bought mother, a concubine, bore me, and yet I was honoured equally with the lawfully born by Castor, son of Hylax,
sentences.n: ὠνητὴ … μήτηρ is ‘a bought mother’: ὠνητός is the verbal adjective of ὠνέομαι ‘buy’, and παλλακίς, in apposition to μήτηρ, is ‘concubine’. τέκε is the unaugmented aorist ‘bore’. ἀλλά με ἶσον ἰθαιγενέεσσιν ἐτίμα is ‘but he honoured me equally with the lawfully born’: ἶσον is the neuter adverb ‘equally’; ἰθαιγενέεσσιν, a dative plural in -εσσι, is explained as ‘straight-born’ (ἰθύς ‘straight’ and the root of γένος), that is legitimate, but the formation is not certain and ‘lawfully born’ is the sense the context gives. The subject Κάστωρ Ὑλακίδης ‘Castor, son of Hylax’ (patronymic in -ίδης) stands at the start of the next line, after the verb that ends this one. The unit ends at the comma after the patronymic; the cut is ours, because the sentence, which has no stop before 206, would otherwise run five lines.

sentences.t:
τοῦ ἐγὼ γένος εὔχομαι εἶναι
ὃς τότ’ ἐνὶ Κρήτεσσι θεὸς ὣς τίετο δήμῳ
ὄλβῳ τε πλούτῳ τε καὶ υἱάσι κυδαλίμοισιν.
sentences.l:
of him I declare myself to be the offspring,
who then among Cretans like a god was honoured in the land
for prosperity and wealth and glorious sons.
sentences.i: whose offspring I declare myself to be, and who in those days was honoured like a god in the land of the Cretans, for his prosperity and wealth and his glorious sons.
sentences.n: τοῦ ἐγὼ γένος εὔχομαι εἶναι is ‘whose offspring I declare myself to be’: τοῦ is the pronoun ‘of him’ (Castor), not a relative, and γένος the predicate of εἶναι. The source prints no stop after εἶναι, and the sentence goes on with ὅς, the relative ‘who’, picking up τοῦ. τότε is ‘then, in those days’, and ἐνὶ Κρήτεσσι ‘among the Cretans’ has the dative plural ending -εσσι. θεὸς ὣς … τίετο is ‘was honoured like a god’, τίετο being the unaugmented imperfect passive of τίω ‘honour’. δήμῳ is ‘in the land’, with δῆμος kept ‘land’ as the house table has it. The datives ὄλβῳ τε πλούτῳ τε καὶ υἱάσι give the grounds of the honour: ὄλβος ‘prosperity’, πλοῦτος ‘wealth’, υἱάσι (= υἱέσι) ‘sons’, with κυδαλίμοισιν ‘glorious’, from κῦδος ‘glory’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι τὸν κῆρες ἔβαν θανάτοιο φέρουσαι
εἰς Ἀΐδαο δόμους·
sentences.l:
But truly him the death-spirits went bearing
to the halls of Hades;
sentences.i: But in truth the spirits of death bore him off to the halls of Hades;
sentences.n: κῆρες is the plural of κήρ ‘death-spirit, doom’, a different word from κῆρ ‘heart’; with θανάτοιο ‘of death’ (-οιο for -ου) it is ‘the death-spirits’ in ‘l’ and ‘the spirits of death’ in ‘i’. φέρουσαι ‘bearing’ agrees with κῆρες, and ἔβαν is the aorist of βαίνω with the old ending -αν (= ἔβησαν), ‘went’. ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι is ‘but in truth’, and τόν is the pronoun ‘him’, Castor, not the article. Ἀΐδαο is the genitive of Ἀΐδης ‘Hades’ in -αο, and εἰς Ἀΐδαο δόμους is ‘to the halls of Hades’, the plural δόμους standing for the one dwelling.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δὲ ζωὴν ἐδάσαντο
παῖδες ὑπέρθυμοι καὶ ἐπὶ κλήρους ἐβάλοντο,
αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ μάλα παῦρα δόσαν καὶ οἰκί’ ἔνειμαν.
sentences.l:
and they the livelihood divided,
the children, high-spirited, and for lots they cast,
but to me very little they gave and dwellings they assigned.
sentences.i: and the high-spirited sons divided the estate among themselves and cast lots for it, but to me they gave very little and assigned a house.
sentences.n: τοί is ‘they’, a pronoun and not the article; the παῖδες ‘children’ in the next line are the sons of the previous lines. ζωήν is not ‘life’ here but ‘livelihood, means of living’, that is the property; ἐδάσαντο is the aorist middle of δατέομαι ‘divide among themselves’. ὑπέρθυμοι keeps its house rendering ‘high-spirited’. ἐπὶ κλήρους ἐβάλοντο is ‘they cast lots’, the middle voice marking that they cast for themselves. ἐμοί ‘to me’ is set against τοί. δόσαν is ἔδοσαν without the augment; οἰκί’ is the elided neuter plural οἰκία ‘dwellings’ (a plural for one dwelling, ‘a house’ in ‘i’), and ἔνειμαν is the aorist of νέμω ‘assign, allot’.

sentences.t:
ἠγαγόμην δὲ γυναῖκα πολυκλήρων ἀνθρώπων
εἵνεκ’ ἐμῆς ἀρετῆς, ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἀποφώλιος ἦα
οὐδὲ φυγοπτόλεμος·
sentences.i: I took a wife from men of many estates, on account of my excellence, since I was no worthless man and no shirker of war;
sentences.n: ἠγαγόμην is the aorist middle of ἄγω, ‘I led home for myself’, the ordinary verb for taking a wife. πολυκλήρων ‘rich in allotments’ (πολύ- and κλῆρος, the lot of land handed down) agrees with ἀνθρώπων. εἵνεκ’ is εἵνεκα (= ἕνεκα) ‘on account of’, with ἐμῆς ἀρετῆς ‘my excellence’, which is a man’s prowess, not his morals. ἀποφώλιος is taken as ‘worthless, good for nothing’; its origin is not known. φυγοπτόλεμος is ‘shunning war’ (φεύγω ‘flee’ and πόλεμος). ἦα is the epic imperfect of εἰμί (= ἦν). The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἤδη πάντα λέλοιπεν
ἀλλ’ ἔμπης καλάμην γέ σ’ ὀΐομαι εἰσορόωντα
γιγνώσκειν·
sentences.i: But now everything has left me; even so, I think you can recognise the stubble by looking at it;
sentences.n: The source prints no stop after λέλοιπεν, so the unit runs on through the next line and ends at the raised dot after γιγνώσκειν. νῦν δ’ ἤδη is ‘but now already’; λέλοιπεν is the perfect of λείπω, ‘has left’ (me is not expressed), with a singular verb after the neuter plural πάντα. ἀλλ’ ἔμπης is ‘yet all the same’. καλάμην is ‘stubble’, the stalks left standing in the field; the picture is that the stubble shows what the crop was. ὀΐομαι ‘I think’ takes σε and the infinitive γιγνώσκειν ‘to know, recognise’, and εἰσορόωντα ‘looking at (it)’ is the uncontracted participle (Attic εἰσορῶντα) agreeing with σ’ = σε.

sentences.t: ἦ γάρ με δύη ἔχει ἤλιθα πολλή.
sentences.l: for truly me affliction holds, abundantly great.
sentences.i: For truly a very great affliction holds me.
sentences.n: ἦ γάρ is ‘for truly’. δύη ‘affliction, misery’ is the subject, με the object, and ἔχει means ‘has hold of’. ἤλιθα is an adverb ‘greatly, abundantly’, and πολλή agrees with δύη, so the two words together press the point: ‘very great indeed’. The clause gives the reason for the stubble: his present misery is what the listener can read.

sentences.t:
ἦ μὲν δὴ θάρσος μοι Ἄρης τ’ ἔδοσαν καὶ Ἀθήνη
καὶ ῥηξηνορίην·
sentences.l:
Truly indeed boldness to me Ares both gave and Athena
and man-breaking-power;
sentences.i: Truly Ares and Athena gave me boldness and the power to break men’s ranks;
sentences.n: ἦ μὲν δή is ‘truly indeed’, an emphatic opening. θάρσος is ‘boldness’. Ἄρης τ’ … καὶ Ἀθήνη is ‘both Ares and Athena’, a double subject with a plural verb, ἔδοσαν, the aorist of δίδωμι. ῥηξηνορίην is a noun built on ῥήγνυμι ‘break’ and ἀνήρ ‘man’ (stem ἀνορ-): ‘man-breaking’, the power to break men’s ranks. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
ὁπότε κρίνοιμι λόχονδε
ἄνδρας ἀριστῆας, κακὰ δυσμενέεσσι φυτεύων,
οὔ ποτέ μοι θάνατον προτιόσσετο θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ,
sentences.l:
whenever I would pick for an ambush
men, the best, evils for enemies planting,
never to me death foresaw the manly spirit,
sentences.i: whenever I picked out the best men for an ambush, devising evil for the enemy, my proud spirit never foresaw my death,
sentences.n: ὁπότε κρίνοιμι is ‘whenever I picked’: ὁπότε with the optative makes a past general clause, something done again and again; κρίνω is ‘choose, pick out’. λόχονδε is ‘to an ambush’ (λόχος ‘ambush’ and the suffix -δε ‘to’). ἄνδρας ἀριστῆας is ‘the best men’, ἀριστῆας being the accusative plural of ἀριστεύς ‘best man, chief’. κακὰ δυσμενέεσσι φυτεύων is ‘planting evils for enemies’ in ‘l’ and ‘devising evil for the enemy’ in ‘i’: φυτεύω is literally ‘plant’, used of contriving harm, and δυσμενέεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι. προτιόσσετο is the unaugmented imperfect of προτιόσσομαι ‘look towards, foresee’, and μοι ‘to me’ does the work of ‘my’. θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ is the house epithet ‘manly spirit’ (‘proud spirit’ in ‘i’), where θυμός is kept ‘spirit’. The unit ends at a comma, the cut being ours: the sentence goes on with ἀλλά in the next unit and would otherwise run five lines.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ πολὺ πρώτιστος ἐπάλμενος ἔγχει ἕλεσκον
ἀνδρῶν δυσμενέων ὅ τέ μοι εἴξειε πόδεσσιν.
sentences.l:
but by far the first, leaping on, with my spear I would take
of hostile men whoever gave way to me with his feet.
sentences.i: but, leaping in by far the first, I would take with my spear whichever of the enemy gave ground before me with his feet.
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ πολὺ πρώτιστος is ‘but by far the first’: πολύ with a superlative is ‘by far’. ἐπάλμενος is the aorist participle of ἐφάλλομαι ‘leap upon’, and ἔγχει is the dative ‘with a spear’. ἕλεσκον is a past iterative of αἱρέω ‘take’ (the suffix -σκ- marks repetition), ‘I would take’, here with the spear, that is bring down. The genitive ἀνδρῶν δυσμενέων is partitive, ‘of the enemy’, and ὅ τέ μοι εἴξειε πόδεσσιν is ‘whoever gave way before me with his feet’, that is, gave ground: ὅ τε is ‘whoever’ with the epic τε, εἴξειε is the optative of εἴκω ‘yield’, and πόδεσσιν is a dative plural ‘with his feet’. The iterative and the optatives together make the whole a description of habit.

sentences.t: τοῖος ἔα ἐν πολέμῳ·
sentences.l: Such was I in war;
sentences.i: Such a man I was in war;
sentences.n: τοῖος ἔα ἐν πολέμῳ is ‘such was I in war’: τοῖος is ‘of such a kind’, pointing back to the picture of 217–221, and ἔα is the epic imperfect of εἰμί (= ἦα, ἦν). The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
ἔργον δέ μοι οὐ φίλον ἔσκεν
οὐδ’ οἰκωφελίη, ἥ τε τρέφει ἀγλαὰ τέκνα,
sentences.l:
but work to me not dear was
nor house-increase, which rears splendid children,
sentences.i: but work was not dear to me, nor the thrift of a household, which rears splendid children,
sentences.n: ἔργον is ‘work’, the toil of farm and household, and ἔσκεν is ἦν with the iterative suffix -σκ-, ‘was, as a rule’; φίλον is ‘dear’. οἰκωφελίη is ‘house-increase’, built on οἶκος ‘house’ and ὀφέλλω ‘increase, benefit’: the careful management by which a household grows. ἥ τε τρέφει ἀγλαὰ τέκνα is ‘which rears splendid children’, the epic τε marking what is generally true, and ἀγλαός kept ‘splendid’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά μοι αἰεὶ νῆες ἐπήρετμοι φίλαι ἦσαν
καὶ πόλεμοι καὶ ἄκοντες ἐΰξεστοι καὶ ὀϊστοί,
λυγρά, τά τ’ ἄλλοισίν γε καταριγηλὰ πέλονται.
sentences.l:
but to me always oared ships dear were
and wars and javelins well-polished and arrows,
grievous things, which to others at least shudder-making are.
sentences.i: but oared ships were always dear to me, and wars, and well-polished javelins and arrows, grievous things that make others shudder.
sentences.n: ἀλλά μοι αἰεί is ‘but to me always’ (αἰεί is Ionic ἀεί). νῆες ἐπήρετμοι is ‘oared ships’: ἐπήρετμος ‘fitted with oars’ is built on ἐπί and ἐρετμόν ‘oar’. φίλαι ἦσαν ‘were dear’ governs the whole list of subjects: ships, wars, javelins and arrows. ἄκοντες is ‘javelins’, ἐΰξεστοι ‘well-polished’, ὀϊστοί ‘arrows’. λυγρά ‘grievous things’ sums the list up (λυγρός is kept ‘grievous’), and τά τ’ ἄλλοισίν γε καταριγηλὰ πέλονται is ‘which, to others at least, are shudder-making’: καταριγηλός is a rare word, usually derived from ῥῖγος ‘chill, shudder’, and its sense is not certain; ‘shudder-making’ follows that derivation. πέλονται is ‘are, become’.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ τὰ φίλ’ ἔσκε τά που θεὸς ἐν φρεσὶ θῆκεν·
sentences.l: but to me those things dear were which perhaps a god in my mind put;
sentences.i: but to me those things were dear which, I suppose, a god put in my mind;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ τὰ φίλ’ ἔσκε is ‘but the things dear to me were’: ἐμοί ‘to me’, φίλα ‘dear’, and ἔσκε the iterative ‘was’ of 222. τά is the relative ‘which’ (= ἅ). που is ‘I suppose, perhaps’, softening the claim that a god did it. θεὸς ἐν φρεσὶ θῆκεν is ‘a god put in my mind’: θῆκεν is the aorist of τίθημι and φρεσί the dative plural of φρήν. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t: ἄλλος γάρ τ’ ἄλλοισιν ἀνὴρ ἐπιτέρπεται ἔργοις.
sentences.l: for one man in different works takes delight.
sentences.i: for one man takes delight in one kind of work, another in another.
sentences.n: ἄλλος … ἄλλοισιν … ἔργοις is the idiom of difference, here ‘one man in one kind of work, another in another’, the ἄλλος of the man answered by the ἄλλοισιν of the works; γάρ gives the reason: tastes differ. τε is the epic τε of a general truth. ἐπιτέρπεται is ‘takes delight in’, with the dative ἔργοις ‘works’, which picks up ἔργον of 222.

sentences.t:
πρὶν μὲν γὰρ Τροίης ἐπιβήμεναι υἷας Ἀχαιῶν
εἰνάκις ἀνδράσιν ἦρξα καὶ ὠκυπόροισι νέεσσιν
ἄνδρας ἐς ἀλλοδαπούς, καί μοι μάλα τύγχανε πολλά.
sentences.l:
For before onto Troy to set foot the sons of the Achaeans
nine times I commanded men and swift-faring ships
to foreign men, and to me very many things fell.
sentences.i: For before the sons of the Achaeans set foot on Troy, nine times I led men and swift-faring ships out to foreign men, and a great deal fell to me.
sentences.n: πρὶν … ἐπιβήμεναι is ‘before … set foot on’: πρίν takes the infinitive, here the aorist ἐπιβήμεναι (Attic ἐπιβῆναι) with the old ending -μεναι, and Τροίης is its genitive object; υἷας Ἀχαιῶν ‘the sons of the Achaeans’ is the accusative subject of the infinitive. εἰνάκις is ‘nine times’. ἀνδράσιν ἦρξα is ‘I led men’: ἄρχω takes the dative. ὠκυπόροισι νέεσσιν is ‘swift-faring ships’, with νέεσσιν the dative plural of νηῦς. ἐς ἀλλοδαπούς is ‘to foreign (men)’. καί μοι μάλα τύγχανε πολλά is ‘and very many things came my way’: the neuter plural πολλά takes the singular τύγχανε ‘happened, fell to my share’.

sentences.t:
τῶν ἐξαιρεύμην μενοεικέα, πολλὰ δ’ ὀπίσσω
λάγχανον·
sentences.l:
of these I would pick out the satisfying things, and many afterwards
I would obtain by lot;
sentences.i: From these I would pick out what satisfied me, and afterwards I would draw many things by lot;
sentences.n: τῶν is ‘of these’, a partitive genitive looking back to the ‘many things’ of 231. ἐξαιρεύμην is the imperfect middle of ἐξαιρέω ‘take out’ (with -εο- written -ευ-, and no augment), ‘I would pick out for myself’: the imperfect says what he did again and again, as λάγχανον does next. μενοεικέα is ‘satisfying’. πολλὰ δ’ ὀπίσσω λάγχανον is ‘and many things afterwards I would obtain by lot’: λαγχάνω is ‘obtain by lot, get as one’s share’, here in the imperfect without augment, and ὀπίσσω is ‘afterwards’. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
αἶψα δὲ οἶκος ὀφέλλετο, καί ῥα ἔπειτα
δεινός τ’ αἰδοῖός τε μετὰ Κρήτεσσι τετύγμην.
sentences.l:
and quickly the house grew, and so then
dread and revered among Cretans I had been made.
sentences.i: My household quickly grew, and so I had become dread and revered among the Cretans.
sentences.n: ὀφέλλετο is the imperfect passive of ὀφέλλω ‘increase’, ‘grew’, the verb of οἰκωφελίη in 223; οἶκος is the house, the household. καί ῥα ἔπειτα is ‘and so then’. δεινός τ’ αἰδοῖός τε is ‘both dread and revered’, two adjectives kept in their house renderings. τετύγμην is the pluperfect passive of τεύχω ‘make’, ‘I had been made, had come to be’, and μετὰ Κρήτεσσι is ‘among the Cretans’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ τήν γε στυγερὴν ὁδὸν εὐρύοπα Ζεὺς
ἐφράσαθ’, ἣ πολλῶν ἀνδρῶν ὑπὸ γούνατ’ ἔλυσε,
δὴ τότ’ ἔμ’ ἤνωγον καὶ ἀγακλυτὸν Ἰδομενῆα
νήεσσ’ ἡγήσασθαι ἐς Ἴλιον·
sentences.l:
But when indeed that hateful journey far-thundering Zeus
devised, which of many men beneath the knees loosed,
then indeed me they urged and renowned Idomeneus
to lead ships to Ilios;
sentences.i: But when Zeus who thunders from afar devised that hateful journey, which loosed the knees of many men, then they urged me and renowned Idomeneus to lead the ships to Ilios;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ … δὴ τότε is ‘but when indeed … then indeed’, a long clause whose main verb, ἤνωγον, comes only in 237. τήν γε στυγερὴν ὁδόν is ‘that hateful journey’: τήν is the demonstrative, γε adds stress, στυγερός is ‘hateful’ and ὁδός ‘way, journey’. εὐρύοπα Ζεύς is the house epithet, ‘far-thundering Zeus’ (‘Zeus who thunders from afar’ in ‘i’); the second element of εὐρύοπα is disputed. ἐφράσαθ’ is the aorist middle of φράζομαι ‘take thought of, devise’. ἣ … ὑπὸ γούνατ’ ἔλυσε is ‘which loosed the knees’, with ὑπὸ … ἔλυσε in tmesis: to loose a man’s knees is to take his strength from him, here by death. ἤνωγον ‘they urged’ is the augmented imperfect of ἀνώγω; ἔμ’ is ἐμέ; ἀγακλυτός is kept ‘renowned’. ἡγήσασθαι ‘to lead’ takes the dative νήεσσ’ ‘the ships’. The unit ends at the raised dot in the middle of 238.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τι μῆχος
ἦεν ἀνήνασθαι, χαλεπὴ δ’ ἔχε δήμου φῆμις.
sentences.l:
and not any remedy
there was to refuse, and harsh held the land’s rumour.
sentences.i: and there was no remedy, no way to refuse, and the talk of the land held us in its harsh grip.
sentences.n: οὐδέ τι μῆχος ἦεν ἀνήνασθαι is ‘and there was no remedy, no way to refuse’: μῆχος is ‘remedy, means of escape’, ἦεν is the epic ἦν, and ἀνήνασθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of ἀναίνομαι ‘refuse’. χαλεπὴ δ’ ἔχε δήμου φῆμις is ‘and harsh talk of the land held (us)’: φῆμις is ‘talk, public voice’, from the root of φημί ‘say’, ἔχε is the imperfect without augment, and its object is not given. δῆμος is kept ‘land’, as in the house table.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα μὲν εἰνάετες πολεμίζομεν υἷες Ἀχαιῶν,
τῷ δεκάτῳ δὲ πόλιν Πριάμου πέρσαντες ἔβημεν
οἴκαδε σὺν νήεσσι, θεὸς δ’ ἐκέδασσεν Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.l:
There for nine years we fought, sons of the Achaeans,
and in the tenth, Priam’s city having sacked, we went
homeward with ships, and a god scattered the Achaeans.
sentences.i: There for nine years we sons of the Achaeans fought, and in the tenth we sacked the city of Priam and went homeward with our ships, and a god scattered the Achaeans.
sentences.n: ἔνθα μέν is ‘there’, and εἰνάετες is the adverb ‘for nine years’. πολεμίζομεν may be a present or an unaugmented imperfect; the English is a past. υἷες Ἀχαιῶν ‘the sons of the Achaeans’ is a stock periphrasis, in apposition to the ‘we’. τῷ δεκάτῳ is ‘in the tenth’, with ἔτει ‘year’ understood. πόλιν Πριάμου πέρσαντες is ‘having sacked the city of Priam’, πέρσαντες being the aorist participle of πέρθω. ἔβημεν is the old aorist ‘we went’ of βαίνω; οἴκαδε is ‘homeward’, with the suffix -δε; σὺν νήεσσι has the dative plural in -εσσι. θεὸς δ’ ἐκέδασσεν Ἀχαιούς is ‘and a god scattered the Achaeans’: ἐκέδασσεν is the aorist of κεδάννυμι (= σκεδάννυμι) ‘scatter’, and the god is not named.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ δειλῷ κακὰ μήδετο μητίετα Ζεύς·
sentences.l: but for me, miserable, evils was devising counsellor Zeus;
sentences.i: but for me, miserable man, Zeus the counsellor was devising evil;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ δειλῷ is ‘but for me, miserable’, δειλῷ being a dative agreeing with ἐμοί (δειλός is kept ‘miserable’). κακὰ μήδετο is ‘was devising evil’, μήδετο being the unaugmented imperfect of μήδομαι ‘plan, devise’. μητίετα is the epic nominative of an epithet of Zeus, ‘counsellor, one who plans’, from μῆτις ‘counsel, cunning’; the nominative in -α is old, like ἱππότα in Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ. The word sits oddly with what the counsellor plans here, and is translated all the same. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
μῆνα γὰρ οἶον ἔμεινα τεταρπόμενος τεκέεσσιν
κουριδίῃ τ’ ἀλόχῳ καὶ κτήμασιν·
sentences.l:
for a month only I stayed, taking delight in my children
and in my wedded wife and possessions;
sentences.i: for I stayed only one month, taking my delight in my children and my wedded wife and my possessions;
sentences.n: μῆνα γὰρ οἶον ἔμεινα is ‘for I stayed only a month’: οἶον is ‘only’, μῆνα an accusative of duration, and γάρ ties the clause to the evils of 243. τεταρπόμενος is the aorist middle participle of τέρπομαι ‘take delight in, have one’s fill of’, with the datives τεκέεσσιν ‘children’ (-εσσι), ἀλόχῳ ‘wife’ and κτήμασιν ‘possessions’. κουριδίῃ … ἀλόχῳ is ‘wedded wife’, the lawful wife. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
Αἴγυπτόνδε με θυμὸς ἀνώγει ναυτίλλεσθαι,
νῆας ἐῢ στείλαντα σὺν ἀντιθέοις ἑτάροισιν.
sentences.l:
but then
to Egypt me my heart urged to sail,
the ships well fitting-out, with godlike companions.
sentences.i: But then my heart urged me to sail to Egypt, once I had fitted out the ships well, with my godlike companions.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα is ‘but then’, opening the next step. Αἴγυπτόνδε is ‘to Egypt’, with the suffix -δε of direction. θυμός is ‘heart’, and ἀνώγει is the imperfect of ἀνώγω, the verb that appeared as ἤνωγον at 237; με is the subject of the infinitive ναυτίλλεσθαι ‘to sail’. νῆας ἐῢ στείλαντα is ‘having fitted out the ships well’: στείλαντα is the aorist participle of στέλλω ‘equip, make ready’, accusative agreeing with με. σὺν ἀντιθέοις ἑτάροισιν is ‘with godlike companions’: ἀντίθεος is kept ‘godlike’ even of ordinary crewmen.

sentences.t: ἐννέα νῆας στεῖλα, θοῶς δ’ ἐσαγείρατο λαός.
sentences.l: nine ships I fitted out, and quickly gathered-in the people.
sentences.i: I fitted out nine ships, and the people quickly assembled.
sentences.n: στεῖλα is the unaugmented aorist of στέλλω, the verb of the previous unit. θοῶς is ‘quickly’, the adverb of θοός ‘swift’. ἐσαγείρατο is the aorist middle of ἀγείρω ‘gather’ with the prefix ἐς-, ‘gathered themselves in’; λαός is ‘people’, a singular noun for the whole body of men with a singular verb.

sentences.t:
ἑξῆμαρ μὲν ἔπειτα ἐμοὶ ἐρίηρες ἑταῖροι
δαίνυντ’·
sentences.l:
For six days then my trusty companions
feasted;
sentences.i: For six days then my trusty companions feasted;
sentences.n: ἑξῆμαρ is the adverb ‘for six days’ (ἕξ and ἦμαρ); ἔπειτα is ‘then’; ἐμοί ‘my’ is a dative of the person concerned. ἐρίηρες ἑταῖροι is ‘trusty companions’, the sense of ἐρίηρος not being fully known. δαίνυντ’ is δαίνυντο, the imperfect middle of δαίνυμι ‘feast’, elided. The first line is a repeat of a published line, and its English is kept. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ἱερήϊα πολλὰ παρεῖχον
θεοῖσίν τε ῥέζειν αὐτοῖσί τε δαῖτα πένεσθαι.
sentences.l:
but I victims many was providing
for the gods to sacrifice, and for themselves a feast to prepare.
sentences.i: while I provided many victims, for them to sacrifice to the gods and to prepare a feast for themselves.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐγών is ‘but I’ (ἐγών is ἐγώ before a vowel here). ἱερήϊα is the neuter plural of ἱερήϊον ‘victim, animal for sacrifice’, the object of παρεῖχον, the imperfect of παρέχω ‘furnish’. The two infinitives say what the animals were for: θεοῖσίν τε ῥέζειν is ‘to sacrifice to the gods’ (ῥέζω is ‘do, perform’, here of ritual), and αὐτοῖσί τε δαῖτα πένεσθαι is ‘and for themselves to prepare a feast’, πένομαι being ‘busy oneself with, get ready’.

sentences.t:
ἑβδομάτῃ δ’ ἀναβάντες ἀπὸ Κρήτης εὐρείης
ἐπλέομεν Βορέῃ ἀνέμῳ ἀκραέϊ καλῷ
ῥηϊδίως, ὡς εἴ τε κατὰ ῥόον·
sentences.i: On the seventh day we put out from broad Crete and sailed with the North Wind, a fresh, fine wind, as easily as if going down a stream;
sentences.n: ἑβδομάτῃ δ’ is ‘and on the seventh’, a dative of time with ἡμέρᾳ ‘day’ understood. ἀναβάντες ἀπὸ Κρήτης εὐρείης is ‘going up from broad Crete’: ἀναβαίνω is ‘go up’, and of a ship ‘go aboard, put out’. ἐπλέομεν is the uncontracted imperfect ‘we were sailing’. Βορέῃ ἀνέμῳ ἀκραέϊ καλῷ is ‘with the North Wind, a fresh, fine wind’: Βορέῃ is the dative (Attic Βορέᾳ), ἀνέμῳ is in apposition, ἀκραής is ‘blowing fresh’ and καλός ‘fine’. ῥηϊδίως is ‘easily’, and ὡς εἴ τε κατὰ ῥόον ‘as if (going) down the stream’. This half-line returns at 299 and its English is kept. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τις οὖν μοι
νηῶν πημάνθη, ἀλλ’ ἀσκηθέες καὶ ἄνουσοι
ἥμεθα, τὰς δ’ ἄνεμός τε κυβερνῆταί τ’ ἴθυνον.
sentences.l:
and not any, then, of my
ships was harmed, but unscathed and free-of-sickness
we sat, and them the wind and the helmsmen guided straight.
sentences.i: and none of my ships was harmed, but we sat unscathed and free from sickness, and the wind and the helmsmen kept the ships straight on their course.
sentences.n: οὐδέ τις οὖν μοι νηῶν πημάνθη is ‘and so not one of my ships was harmed’: οὖν is ‘so’, μοι ‘of mine’, νηῶν a partitive genitive, and πημάνθη the aorist passive of πημαίνω, from πῆμα ‘woe’. ἀσκηθέες ‘unscathed’ and ἄνουσοι ‘free from sickness’ (ἀ- and νόσος) belong to the ‘we’ of ἥμεθα ‘we sat’, the imperfect of ἦμαι. The last line is a stock line, and its English is kept: τάς is ‘them’, the ships, and ἴθυνον the imperfect of ἰθύνω ‘steer straight’.

sentences.t:
πεμπταῖοι δ’ Αἴγυπτον ἐϋρρείτην ἱκόμεσθα,
στῆσα δ’ ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ ποταμῷ νέας ἀμφιελίσσας.
sentences.l:
On the fifth day Egypt, fair-flowing, we reached,
and I halted in the river Egypt the ships, both-sides-curving.
sentences.i: On the fifth day we reached fair-flowing Egypt, and I halted my ships, curved on both sides, in the river Egypt.
sentences.n: πεμπταῖοι is an adjective doing the work of an adverb, ‘as fifth-day men’, that is ‘on the fifth day’; it agrees with the ‘we’ of ἱκόμεσθα (= ἱκόμεθα). Αἴγυπτον ἐϋρρείτην is ‘fair-flowing Egypt’: ἐϋρρείτης is built on ἐῢ ‘fair’ and ῥέω ‘flow’, a river-word, and ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ ποταμῷ in the next line is ‘in the river Egypt’, so here the name belongs to the river; it also names the land, as in Αἴγυπτόνδε at 246. στῆσα is the unaugmented aorist ‘I halted’; νέας is νῆας. ἀμφιελίσσας is ‘curved on both sides’, a sense that is disputed, ‘rowed on both sides’ being another guess.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἦ τοι μὲν ἐγὼ κελόμην ἐρίηρας ἑταίρους
αὐτοῦ πὰρ νήεσσι μένειν καὶ νῆας ἔρυσθαι,
ὀπτῆρας δὲ κατὰ σκοπιὰς ὤτρυνα νέεσθαι·
sentences.i: There I ordered my trusty companions to stay right where they were by the ships and guard them, and I urged scouts to go to the lookout points;
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ ἦ τοι μὲν ἐγώ is ‘there I on my part’: the μέν is answered by the δέ of the third line, which sets the order to the sailors against the order to the scouts. κελόμην is the unaugmented imperfect of κέλομαι ‘order, urge’. ἐρίηρας ἑταίρους ‘trusty companions’ are the accusative subject of the infinitives μένειν ‘to stay’ and ἔρυσθαι ‘to guard’ (from ἐρύομαι ‘protect’). αὐτοῦ is ‘right there’. ὀπτῆρας is ‘scouts’, κατὰ σκοπιάς ‘to the lookouts’, ὤτρυνα the aorist of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, and νέεσθαι ‘to go’ the infinitive of νέομαι. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ὕβρει εἴξαντες, ἐπισπόμενοι μένεϊ σφῷ,
αἶψα μάλ’ Αἰγυπτίων ἀνδρῶν περικαλλέας ἀγροὺς
πόρθεον, ἐκ δὲ γυναῖκας ἄγον καὶ νήπια τέκνα,
αὐτούς τ’ ἔκτεινον·
sentences.l:
But they, to insolence having yielded, following their own strength,
at once, very quickly, of Egyptian men the very fair fields
were ravaging, and out women they led and infant children,
and the men themselves they killed;
sentences.i: But they gave way to insolence and, following their own strength, at once began to ravage the very fair fields of the Egyptian men, carrying off women and little children and killing the men themselves;
sentences.n: οἱ δ’ ὕβρει εἴξαντες is ‘but they, having yielded to insolence’: οἱ is ‘they’, and ὕβρις ‘insolence, wanton violence’ is the dative after the aorist participle of εἴκω ‘yield’. ἐπισπόμενοι μένεϊ σφῷ is ‘following their own strength’: ἐπισπόμενοι is the aorist middle participle of ἐφέπομαι ‘follow’, and σφῷ is the possessive ‘their own’, not a pronoun. αἶψα μάλ’ is ‘very quickly’; περικαλλέας ἀγρούς is ‘very fair fields’, with περικαλλής kept ‘very fair’; πόρθεον is the uncontracted imperfect of πορθέω ‘ravage’. ἐκ … ἄγον is tmesis for ἐξῆγον ‘led out’, and νήπια τέκνα is ‘infant children’, νήπιος being ‘without speech, infant’. αὐτούς τ’ ἔκτεινον is ‘and the men themselves they killed’. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t: τάχα δ’ ἐς πόλιν ἵκετ’ ἀϋτή.
sentences.l: and quickly to the city came the cry.
sentences.i: and soon the cry reached the city.
sentences.n: τάχα is ‘quickly, soon’ and ἐς πόλιν ‘to the city’. ἵκετ’ is ἵκετο, a past tense of ἱκνέομαι ‘come’; the ι is long here, and that long ι is the augment. ἀϋτή is ‘a cry, an outcry’, the noise of the raid carrying to the town.

sentences.t:
οἱ δὲ βοῆς ἀΐοντες ἅμ’ ἠοῖ φαινομένηφιν
ἦλθον·
sentences.l:
And they, the shout hearing, with dawn appearing
came;
sentences.i: And hearing the shout, they came as dawn appeared;
sentences.n: οἱ δέ is ‘and they’, the people of the city. βοῆς ἀΐοντες is ‘hearing the shout’: ἀΐω takes a genitive of what is heard. ἅμ’ ἠοῖ φαινομένηφιν is ‘with dawn appearing’: ἅμα takes the dative ἠοῖ, and φαινομένηφιν is the participle with the old ending -φιν, standing where a dative φαινομένῃ would. The unit ends at the raised dot after ἦλθον.

sentences.t:
πλῆτο δὲ πᾶν πεδίον πεζῶν τε καὶ ἵππων
χαλκοῦ τε στεροπῆς·
sentences.l:
and was filled the whole plain with footmen and horses
and the flash of bronze;
sentences.i: and the whole plain was filled with foot soldiers and horses and the flash of bronze;
sentences.n: πλῆτο is the aorist of πίμπλημι ‘fill’ in the passive sense, ‘was filled’, with the genitives πεζῶν ‘foot soldiers’ and ἵππων ‘horses’; πᾶν πεδίον is ‘the whole plain’. χαλκοῦ τε στεροπῆς is ‘and the flash of bronze’: στεροπή is ‘flash’, the word used of lightning, here the glint of weapons and armour. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
ἐν δὲ Ζεὺς τερπικέραυνος
φύζαν ἐμοῖς ἑτάροισι κακὴν βάλεν, οὐδέ τις ἔτλη
μεῖναι ἐναντίβιον·
sentences.i: and Zeus, who delights in the thunderbolt, cast a terrible panic into my companions, and not one brought himself to stand against them;
sentences.n: ἐν δὲ … βάλεν is tmesis for ἐνέβαλεν ‘cast into’, βάλεν being the unaugmented aorist. Ζεὺς τερπικέραυνος is ‘Zeus who delights in the thunderbolt’ (‘bolt-delighting Zeus’ in ‘l’), from τέρπω ‘delight’ and κεραυνός ‘thunderbolt’. φύζαν … κακήν is ‘an evil panic’: φύζα is ‘flight, rout’, the fear that sends men running; κακός is ‘evil’ in ‘l’ and ‘terrible’ in ‘i’. ἔτλη is the aorist of τλάω ‘endure’, ‘brought himself to’, with the infinitive μεῖναι ‘to await, stand against’; ἐναντίβιον is ‘in opposition, face to face’, an adverb built on ἐναντίος and βίη ‘force’. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t: περὶ γὰρ κακὰ πάντοθεν ἔστη.
sentences.l: for around evils from every side stood.
sentences.i: for evils stood round them on every side.
sentences.n: περὶ … ἔστη is tmesis for περιέστη ‘stood around’. κακά ‘evils’ is a neuter plural with a singular verb, and πάντοθεν is ‘from all sides’, with the suffix -θεν. The clause gives the reason (γάρ) for the panic.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἡμέων πολλοὺς μὲν ἀπέκτανον ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ,
τοὺς δ’ ἄναγον ζωούς, σφίσιν ἐργάζεσθαι ἀνάγκῃ.
sentences.l:
Then of us many they killed with sharp bronze,
and the others they led up alive, for themselves to work by compulsion.
sentences.i: Then they killed many of us with the sharp bronze, and the others they led away alive, to work for them under compulsion.
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ is ‘then, thereupon’. ἡμέων is ἡμῶν ‘of us’, partitive after πολλούς ‘many’, the object of ἀπέκτανον ‘they killed’, a second aorist of κτείνω with the ending -ον. ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ is ‘with sharp bronze’, the metal standing for the weapon, as in 268. τοὺς δ’ is ‘but the others’, a demonstrative contrasted with πολλούς; ἄναγον is ‘they led up’ and ζωούς ‘alive’. σφίσιν is the dative ‘for them’, ἐργάζεσθαι ‘to work’, and ἀνάγκῃ ‘under compulsion’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ Ζεὺς αὐτὸς ἐνὶ φρεσὶν ὧδε νόημα
ποίησ’—ὡς ὄφελον θανέειν καὶ πότμον ἐπισπεῖν
αὐτοῦ ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ·
sentences.i: But Zeus himself put such a thought in my mind—would that I had died and met my doom there in Egypt;
sentences.n: ποίησ’ is ποίησε ‘made, put’: ‘Zeus himself made such a thought in my mind’. ὧδε ‘thus’ points forward to the act of the next unit, and νόημα is ‘thought, plan’. After the dash comes a parenthesis, which runs on into the next unit: ὡς ὄφελον θανέειν is ‘would that I had died’, ὄφελον being the aorist of ὀφέλλω ‘owe’ used as a wish for what cannot now be; θανέειν is the uncontracted aorist infinitive of θνῄσκω. πότμον ἐπισπεῖν is ‘to meet my doom’, ἐπισπεῖν being the aorist infinitive of ἐφέπω ‘follow, undergo’. αὐτοῦ ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ is ‘right there in Egypt’. The unit ends at the raised dot in the middle of 275; the cut is ours, because the sentence would otherwise run five lines.

sentences.t:
ἔτι γάρ νύ με πῆμ’ ὑπέδεκτο—
αὐτίκ’ ἀπὸ κρατὸς κυνέην εὔτυκτον ἔθηκα
καὶ σάκος ὤμοιϊν, δόρυ δ’ ἔκβαλον ἔκτοσε χειρός·
sentences.i: for woe was still waiting to receive me—at once I took the well-made helmet from my head and the shield from my shoulders, and threw the spear away out of my hand;
sentences.n: ἔτι γάρ νύ με πῆμ’ ὑπέδεκτο closes the parenthesis and is literally ‘for still woe received me’: ὑπέδεκτο is the aorist of ὑποδέχομαι ‘receive, take under’, and a past ‘received’ sits oddly with ‘still’; ‘was waiting to receive me’ is a reading from the sense, and the tense is not clearly explained. νύ is a particle ‘now, indeed’. The main clause then goes on: αὐτίκ’ ἀπὸ κρατὸς … ἔθηκα is ‘at once I put off from my head’, with ἀπὸ … ἔθηκα in tmesis for ἀπέθηκα; κρατός is the genitive of κάρη ‘head’ (stem κρατ-). κυνέην εὔτυκτον is ‘a well-made helmet’: κυνέη, from κύων ‘dog’, was first a cap of dog-skin, and εὔτυκτος is ‘well-wrought’, from the root of τεύχω. καὶ σάκος ὤμοιϊν is ‘and the shield from my shoulders’: ὤμοιϊν is read as a dual, ‘from my two shoulders’, taken as a genitive with the ἀπὸ of ἀπὸ … ἔθηκα carried over; the case is not certain. δόρυ δ’ ἔκβαλον ἔκτοσε χειρός is ‘and the spear I threw out away from my hand’: ἔκτοσε is ‘out, away’ and χειρός a genitive of separation. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ βασιλῆος ἐναντίον ἤλυθον ἵππων
καὶ κύσα γούναθ’ ἑλών·
sentences.l:
but I in front of the king’s horses came
and kissed his knees, having taken hold;
sentences.i: I came before the king’s horses, and taking hold of his knees I kissed them;
sentences.n: βασιλῆος … ἵππων is ‘the king’s horses’, the two words split by ἐναντίον ‘in front of’. ἤλυθον is the epic aorist of ἔρχομαι (= ἦλθον). κύσα is the unaugmented aorist of κυνέω ‘kiss’, and γούναθ’ is γούνατα ‘knees’: to take a man by the knees is the gesture of a suppliant, begging his protection. ἑλών is the aorist participle of αἱρέω, ‘having taken (hold of)’, and γούναθ’ is the object of both verbs. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
ὁδ’ ἐρύσατο καί μ’ ἐλέησεν,
ἐς δίφρον δέ μ’ ἕσας ἄγεν οἴκαδε δάκρυ χέοντα.
sentences.l:
but he rescued me and pitied me,
and into his chariot having seated me led me homeward, a tear shedding.
sentences.i: But he saved me and took pity on me, and he seated me in his chariot and took me homeward as I shed tears.
sentences.n: ὁδ’ is ὁ δ’ ‘but he’, a pronoun, the king being the subject. ἐρύσατο is the aorist middle of ἐρύομαι ‘protect, rescue’, the verb of ἔρυσθαι at 260; ἐλέησεν is the aorist of ἐλεέω ‘pity’, without the lengthened augment. ἐς δίφρον δέ μ’ ἕσας is ‘and having seated me in his chariot’: ἕσας is the aorist participle of the causative of ἵζω ‘seat’, and δίφρος is the chariot. ἄγεν is the unaugmented imperfect ‘took’, and οἴκαδε ‘homeward’. δάκρυ χέοντα is the house phrase ‘shedding tears’, in the accusative to agree with μ’: it was Odysseus who wept.

sentences.t:
ἦ μέν μοι μάλα πολλοὶ ἐπήϊσσον μελίῃσιν,
ἱέμενοι κτεῖναι—δὴ γὰρ κεχολώατο λίην—
ἀλλ’ ἀπὸ κεῖνος ἔρυκε, Διὸς δ’ ὠπίζετο μῆνιν
ξεινίου, ὅς τε μάλιστα νεμεσσᾶται κακὰ ἔργα.
sentences.l:
Truly indeed at me very many were rushing with ash-spears,
eager to kill—for indeed they were angry exceedingly—
but he kept them off, and of Zeus he held in awe the wrath,
the guest-god’s, who most of all is indignant at evil deeds.
sentences.i: Truly, very many rushed at me with their ash spears, eager to kill me—for they were exceedingly angry—but he kept them off, and stood in awe of the wrath of Zeus, the god of guests, who is most of all indignant at evil deeds.
sentences.n: ἦ μέν is ‘truly indeed’, as at 216. ἐπήϊσσον is the imperfect of ἐπαΐσσω ‘rush at’, with the dative μοι ‘at me’; μελίῃσιν is the dative plural of μελίη, the ash tree and the spear made of its wood. ἱέμενοι κτεῖναι is ‘eager to kill’. Between the dashes, δὴ γὰρ κεχολώατο λίην is ‘for they were exceedingly angry’, κεχολώατο being the pluperfect middle of χολόομαι ‘be angry’ with the ending -ατο for -ντο. ἀλλ’ ἀπὸ κεῖνος ἔρυκε is ‘but he kept them off’: ἀπὸ … ἔρυκε is tmesis for ἀπέρυκε, and κεῖνος is Ionic ἐκεῖνος ‘that man’, the king. Διὸς δ’ ὠπίζετο μῆνιν ξεινίου is ‘and he stood in awe of the wrath of Zeus, god of guests’: ὀπίζομαι is ‘have regard for, fear’, μῆνις ‘wrath’, and ξείνιος ‘of guests’, the epithet of Zeus as the one who watches over the treatment of strangers. ὅς τε μάλιστα νεμεσσᾶται κακὰ ἔργα is ‘who is most of all indignant at evil deeds’: νεμεσσάομαι is ‘feel righteous anger at’, and τε marks what is generally so.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα μὲν ἑπτάετες μένον αὐτόθι, πολλὰ δ’ ἄγειρα
χρήματ’ ἀν’ Αἰγυπτίους ἄνδρας·
sentences.l:
There for seven years I stayed on the spot, and many I gathered
goods among the Egyptian men;
sentences.i: There I stayed on the spot for seven years, and I gathered many goods among the Egyptians;
sentences.n: ἔνθα μέν is ‘there’, and ἑπτάετες is ‘for seven years’, an adverb like εἰνάετες at 240. μένον is the unaugmented imperfect ‘I stayed’; αὐτόθι is ‘right there’, with the suffix -θι of place. ἄγειρα is the unaugmented aorist of ἀγείρω ‘gather’, and χρήματ’ is ‘goods’. ἀν’ Αἰγυπτίους ἄνδρας is ‘among the Egyptian men’, ἀνά with the accusative meaning ‘up and down among’. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t: δίδοσαν γὰρ ἅπαντες.
sentences.l: for they gave, all.
sentences.i: for they all gave.
sentences.n: δίδοσαν is ἐδίδοσαν without the augment, the imperfect of δίδωμι, ‘they gave’ and so ‘kept giving’. γάρ says how he was able to gather so much, and ἅπαντες is ‘all’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ ὄγδοόν μοι ἐπιπλόμενον ἔτος ἦλθεν,
δὴ τότε Φοῖνιξ ἦλθεν ἀνὴρ ἀπατήλια εἰδώς,
τρώκτης, ὃς δὴ πολλὰ κάκ’ ἀνθρώποισιν ἐώργει·
sentences.i: But when the eighth year came round for me, then a Phoenician came, a man versed in deceits, a rogue who had done men many evils;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ … δὴ τότε again frames the clause. ὄγδοόν μοι ἐπιπλόμενον ἔτος ἦλθεν is ‘the eighth year came round for me’: ἐπιπλόμενον comes from ἐπιπέλομαι ‘come on, come round’ and agrees with ἔτος. Φοῖνιξ … ἀνήρ is ‘a Phoenician man’. ἀπατήλια εἰδώς is ‘knowing deceits’: ἀπατήλιος ‘deceitful’ is used as a neuter plural noun, and εἰδώς with the accusative is ‘versed in’, as in πεπνυμένα μήδεα εἰδώς. τρώκτης is ‘a gnawer’, from τρώγω ‘gnaw’, usually taken to mean ‘rogue, cheat’; its sense is not secure. ὃς δὴ πολλὰ κάκ’ ἀνθρώποισιν ἐώργει is ‘who had indeed done many evils to men’: ἐώργει is the pluperfect of ἔρδω ‘do’, and κάκ’ is κακά elided. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
ὅς μ’ ἄγε παρπεπιθὼν ᾗσι φρεσίν, ὄφρ’ ἱκόμεσθα
Φοινίκην, ὅθι τοῦ γε δόμοι καὶ κτήματ’ ἔκειτο.
sentences.l:
who led me, having won me over with his own wits, until we came
to Phoenicia, where his house and possessions lay.
sentences.i: He won me over with his own wits and led me away, until we reached Phoenicia, where his house and possessions lay.
sentences.n: ὅς μ’ ἄγε is ‘who led me’: ὅς is the relative and ἄγε the unaugmented imperfect of ἄγω. παρπεπιθών is the aorist participle of πείθω with the prefix παρα-, ‘talking round, winning over’. ᾗσι φρεσίν is ‘with his own wits’: ᾗσι is the dative plural of the possessive ἥ ‘his own’, not the relative. ὄφρ’ ἱκόμεσθα is ‘until we reached’ (ἱκόμεσθα = ἱκόμεθα), with Φοινίκην ‘Phoenicia’ as its object in the next line. ὅθι is ‘where’, and τοῦ γε ‘his’. δόμοι καὶ κτήματ’ ἔκειτο is ‘his house and possessions lay’: ἔκειτο, the imperfect of κεῖμαι, is singular, agreeing with the nearer neuter plural κτήματα.

sentences.t: ἔνθα παρ’ αὐτῷ μεῖνα τελεσφόρον εἰς ἐνιαυτόν.
sentences.l: There beside him I stayed for a completion-bearing year.
sentences.i: There I stayed with him for a full year.
sentences.n: ἔνθα παρ’ αὐτῷ is ‘there beside him’, the Phoenician being the one meant. μεῖνα is the unaugmented aorist of μένω ‘stay’. τελεσφόρον is ‘bearing completion’ (τέλος ‘end’ and φέρω ‘bear’): a year that carries itself through to its end, hence ‘full’ in ‘i’; εἰς ἐνιαυτόν is ‘for a year’. The next unit counts the year out.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ μῆνές τε καὶ ἡμέραι ἐξετελεῦντο
ἄψ περιτελλομένου ἔτεος καὶ ἐπήλυθον ὧραι,
sentences.l:
But when indeed the months and the days were completed,
as the year went round again, and the seasons came on,
sentences.i: But when the months and the days were completed, as the year came round again and the seasons came on,
sentences.n: These two lines are stock lines, and their English is kept. ἐξετελεῦντο is the imperfect passive of ἐκτελέω ‘bring to an end’, ‘were being completed’. ἄψ is ‘back, again’, with the genitive absolute περιτελλομένου ἔτεος ‘the year coming round’; ἐπήλυθον is the epic aorist of ἐπέρχομαι ‘come on’, and ὧραι ‘seasons’. The unit ends at a comma, because the whole sentence runs five lines.

sentences.t:
ἐς Λιβύην μ’ ἐπὶ νηὸς ἐέσσατο ποντοπόροιο
ψεύδεα βουλεύσας, ἵνα οἱ σὺν φόρτον ἄγοιμι,
κεῖθι δέ μ’ ὡς περάσειε καὶ ἄσπετον ὦνον ἕλοιτο.
sentences.l:
to Libya me on a ship, sea-crossing, he put aboard,
lies having planned, so that with him a cargo I might bring,
and there that he might sell me and a boundless price take.
sentences.i: he put me aboard a sea-crossing ship for Libya, having planned lies, so that I would bring a cargo along with him, and so that there he could sell me and take a boundless price.
sentences.n: ἐς Λιβύην is ‘to Libya’, and ἐπὶ νηὸς ποντοπόροιο ‘on a sea-crossing ship’, with -οιο for -ου; ποντοπόρος is built on πόντος ‘open sea’ and πόρος ‘passage’. ἐέσσατο is taken as the aorist middle of the causative of ἵζω, ‘made me sit, put me aboard’, from the same family as ἕσας at 280; the form is unusual and the sense comes from the context. ψεύδεα βουλεύσας is ‘having planned lies’. The two purpose clauses follow: ἵνα οἱ σὺν φόρτον ἄγοιμι is ‘so that I might bring a cargo along with him’ (σύν is adverbial and οἱ is ‘him’), and ὡς … περάσειε καὶ … ἕλοιτο is ‘and that he might sell me and take’, περάω being ‘sell abroad’. ἄσπετον ὦνον is ‘a boundless price’: ἄσπετος is literally ‘not to be told’, and is kept ‘boundless’, its house rendering; ἕλοιτο is the optative middle of αἱρέω.

sentences.t: τῷ ἑπόμην ἐπὶ νηός, ὀϊόμενός περ, ἀνάγκῃ.
sentences.l: him I followed onto the ship, suspecting though, under compulsion.
sentences.i: I followed him aboard the ship, though I had my suspicions, under compulsion.
sentences.n: τῷ ἑπόμην ἐπὶ νηός is ‘him I followed onto the ship’: τῷ is the pronoun ‘him’, the dative after ἕπομαι, and ἐπὶ νηός is ‘onto the ship’. ὀϊόμενός περ is ‘though suspecting’: ὀΐομαι is ‘suppose, expect’, here of something feared, and περ makes the participle concessive. ἀνάγκῃ is ‘under compulsion’, as at 272.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ἔθεεν Βορέῃ ἀνέμῳ ἀκραέϊ καλῷ,
μέσσον ὑπὲρ Κρήτης·
sentences.l:
And she ran with the North Wind, a fresh, fine wind,
midway above Crete;
sentences.i: The ship ran with the North Wind, a fresh, fine wind, midway above Crete;
sentences.n: ἡ δ’ is ‘and she’, the ship. ἔθεεν is the uncontracted imperfect of θέω ‘run’, said of a ship. The half-line Βορέῃ ἀνέμῳ ἀκραέϊ καλῷ is the same as at 253, and its English is kept. μέσσον ὑπὲρ Κρήτης is rendered literally ‘midway above Crete’; the sense is not clear, since ὑπέρ with the genitive is ‘over, above’, μέσσον is ‘in the middle’, and the line gives no more exact picture of the ship’s course. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t: Ζεὺς δέ σφισι μήδετ’ ὄλεθρον.
sentences.l: but Zeus for them was devising destruction.
sentences.i: but Zeus was devising destruction for them.
sentences.n: σφισι is the dative plural pronoun ‘for them’, those aboard the ship. μήδετ’ is μήδετο, the same imperfect as at 243, ‘was devising’. ὄλεθρον is ‘destruction’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ Κρήτην μὲν ἐλείπομεν, οὐδέ τις ἄλλη
φαίνετο γαιάων, ἀλλ’ οὐρανὸς ἠδὲ θάλασσα,
δὴ τότε κυανέην νεφέλην ἔστησε Κρονίων
νηὸς ὕπερ γλαφυρῆς, ἤχλυσε δὲ πόντος ὑπ’ αὐτῆς.
sentences.l:
But when indeed Crete we were leaving, and no other
land appeared, but sky and sea,
then indeed a dark cloud the son of Cronus set
over the hollow ship, and the open-sea grew dim beneath it.
sentences.i: But when we left Crete behind, and no other land came into sight, only sky and sea, then the son of Cronus set a dark cloud above the hollow ship, and the sea grew dim beneath it.
sentences.n: These lines repeat a published passage, with ‘Crete’ where the other has ‘the island’, and the English of the rest is kept. ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ … δὴ τότε is ‘but when indeed … then indeed’ again. The μέν of Κρήτην μέν is answered by οὐδέ τις ἄλλη ‘and no other’. ἐλείπομεν is ‘we were leaving’, and γαιάων is the genitive plural of γαῖα, partitive with τις ἄλλη, ‘no other of lands’. κυανέην νεφέλην is ‘a dark cloud’; Κρονίων is ‘the son of Cronus’, a patronymic; γλαφυρῆς is ‘hollow’ and ἤχλυσε ‘grew dim’.

sentences.t: Ζεὺς δ’ ἄμυδις βρόντησε καὶ ἔμβαλε νηῒ κεραυνόν·
sentences.l: And Zeus at once thundered and cast on the ship a thunderbolt;
sentences.i: At the same moment Zeus thundered and hurled a thunderbolt into the ship;
sentences.n: ἄμυδις is ‘all at once, at the same time’. βρόντησε is the aorist of βροντάω ‘thunder’, and ἔμβαλε is ‘cast into, hurled at’, taking the dative νηῒ ‘the ship’, written with a diaeresis (= νηΐ). The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ἐλελίχθη πᾶσα Διὸς πληγεῖσα κεραυνῷ,
ἐν δὲ θεείου πλῆτο·
sentences.l:
and she shook all over, struck by the thunderbolt of Zeus,
and with sulphur was filled;
sentences.i: She shook from end to end, struck by the thunderbolt of Zeus, and was filled with sulphur;
sentences.n: These two lines are repeated from a published passage, and their English is kept. ἐλελίχθη is the aorist passive of ἐλελίζω ‘shake, whirl’, πᾶσα is ‘all over’ (the whole ship), and πληγεῖσα is the aorist passive participle of πλήσσω ‘strike’; Διὸς … κεραυνῷ is ‘by the thunderbolt of Zeus’. In ἐν δὲ θεείου πλῆτο the ἐν is adverbial, ‘in it’, and θεείου is a genitive ‘of sulphur’, θέειον being sulphur. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t: πέσον δ’ ἐκ νηὸς ἅπαντες.
sentences.l: and fell from the ship all.
sentences.i: and they all fell out of the ship.
sentences.n: πέσον is the unaugmented aorist of πίπτω (= ἔπεσον), ‘they fell’. ἐκ νηός is ‘out of the ship’, and ἅπαντες ‘all’ is the nominative with the verb: every man aboard.

sentences.t:
οἱ δὲ κορώνῃσιν ἴκελοι περὶ νῆα μέλαιναν
κύμασιν ἐμφορέοντο·
sentences.l:
and they, like crows, around the black ship
on the waves were carried about;
sentences.i: And they, like crows, were carried about the black ship on the waves;
sentences.n: οἱ δέ is ‘and they’. κορώνῃσιν ἴκελοι is ‘like crows’: ἴκελος ‘like’ takes the dative, and κορώνη is ‘crow’. περὶ νῆα μέλαιναν is ‘about the black ship’, μέλας being kept ‘black’ of ships. κύμασιν is ‘on the waves’, and ἐμφορέοντο ‘were carried about’, the imperfect passive of a verb meaning ‘carry about, toss’. The line is a stock line, and its English is kept. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t: θεὸς δ’ ἀποαίνυτο νόστον.
sentences.l: and the god took away their homecoming.
sentences.i: and the god took away their homecoming.
sentences.n: θεὸς δ’ ἀποαίνυτο νόστον is ‘and the god took away their homecoming’: the god is Zeus, named at 305, and ἀποαίνυτο is the unaugmented imperfect middle of ἀπαίνυμαι ‘take away’. νόστον is ‘homecoming’. This is the second half of a stock line, and its English is kept.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ Ζεὺς αὐτός, ἔχοντί περ ἄλγεα θυμῷ,
ἱστὸν ἀμαιμάκετον νηὸς κυανοπρῴροιο
ἐν χείρεσσιν ἔθηκεν, ὅπως ἔτι πῆμα φύγοιμι.
sentences.l:
but to me Zeus himself, though having pains in my heart,
a mast, huge, of the dark-prowed ship
into my hands put, so that still woe I might escape.
sentences.i: But Zeus himself, though I was beset by pains in my heart, put into my hands the huge mast of the dark-prowed ship, so that I might yet escape woe.
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ Ζεὺς αὐτός is ‘but for me Zeus himself’. ἔχοντί περ ἄλγεα θυμῷ is ‘though (I was) having pains in my heart’: ἔχοντι is the dative participle agreeing with ἐμοί, θυμῷ is ‘in my heart’ (θυμός kept ‘heart’), and περ makes it concessive. ἱστόν is ‘mast’ (ἱστός also means ‘loom’). ἀμαιμάκετον is an epithet of unknown meaning, guessed at as ‘huge’ or ‘irresistible’; both layers read ‘huge’. νηὸς κυανοπρῴροιο is ‘of the dark-prowed ship’, and ἐν χείρεσσιν ἔθηκεν ‘put in my hands’. ὅπως ἔτι πῆμα φύγοιμι is ‘so that I might yet escape woe’, an optative of purpose after a past verb.

sentences.t: τῷ ῥα περιπλεχθεὶς φερόμην ὀλοοῖς ἀνέμοισιν.
sentences.l: to it then wrapped-around I was carried by deadly winds.
sentences.i: Wrapped around it, I was carried along by the deadly winds.
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘it’, the mast. περιπλεχθείς is the aorist passive participle of περιπλέκω ‘twine round, clasp’, so ‘wrapped around it’. φερόμην is the imperfect passive of φέρω, ‘I was carried’, and ὀλοοῖς ἀνέμοισιν is ‘by deadly winds’, a dative of means, with ὀλοός kept ‘deadly’.

sentences.t:
ἐννῆμαρ φερόμην, δεκάτῃ δέ με νυκτὶ μελαίνῃ
γαίῃ Θεσπρωτῶν πέλασεν μέγα κῦμα κυλίνδον.
sentences.l:
For nine days I was carried, and on the tenth me, in black night,
to the land of the Thesprotians brought near a great wave, rolling me.
sentences.i: For nine days I was carried along, and on the tenth, in the dark night, a great wave, rolling me, brought me to the land of the Thesprotians.
sentences.n: ἐννῆμαρ is ‘for nine days’, an adverb like εἰνάετες and ἑπτάετες, and φερόμην repeats the verb of 313. δεκάτῃ δέ με νυκτὶ μελαίνῃ is ‘and on the tenth night, a dark one, me’: δεκάτῃ agrees with νυκτί, a dative of time, with νὺξ μέλαινα kept ‘dark night’ in ‘i’ and ‘black night’ in ‘l’. γαίῃ Θεσπρωτῶν is ‘to the land of the Thesprotians’, a dative of direction after πέλασεν ‘brought near’. μέγα κῦμα κυλίνδον is ‘a great wave, rolling (me)’: κυλίνδον is the neuter present participle of κυλίνδω, with με understood from the line before.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα με Θεσπρωτῶν βασιλεὺς ἐκομίσσατο Φείδων
ἥρως ἀπριάτην·
sentences.l:
There me the Thesprotians’ king took in, Pheidon,
the hero, unbought;
sentences.i: There Pheidon, king of the Thesprotians, the hero, took me into his care without price;
sentences.n: ἔνθα με … ἐκομίσσατο is ‘there … took me in’: ἐκομίσσατο is the aorist middle of κομίζω ‘take care of, receive’. Θεσπρωτῶν βασιλεὺς … Φείδων is ‘Pheidon, king of the Thesprotians’; ἥρως is the title ‘the hero’. ἀπριάτην is the feminine accusative singular of ἀπρίατος ‘unbought’; with no noun to agree with it works as an adverb, ‘without price’, the usual explanation, though not certain: he took the stranger in and asked nothing for it. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
τοῦ γὰρ φίλος υἱὸς ἐπελθὼν
αἴθρῳ καὶ καμάτῳ δεδμημένον ἦγεν ἐς οἶκον,
χειρὸς ἀναστήσας, ὄφρ’ ἵκετο δώματα πατρός·
ἀμφὶ δέ με χλαῖνάν τε χιτῶνά τε εἵματα ἕσσεν.
sentences.i: for his dear son came upon me, overcome by cold and weariness, and led me to the house, raising me by the hand, until he reached his father’s halls; and he put clothes about me, a cloak and a tunic.
sentences.n: τοῦ γὰρ φίλος υἱός is ‘for his dear son’: τοῦ is ‘his’, the king’s. ἐπελθών is ‘having come upon (me)’, and δεδμημένον, the perfect passive participle of δάμνημι ‘overpower’, agrees with με: αἴθρῳ καὶ καμάτῳ is ‘by cold and by weariness’. αἴθρῳ is a dative of a word related to αἴθρη ‘clear sky’, here understood as the cold that comes with clear air; that sense is not certain. ἦγεν ἐς οἶκον is ‘led me to the house’, and χειρὸς ἀναστήσας ‘having raised me by the hand’, with the genitive of the part taken hold of. ὄφρ’ ἵκετο δώματα πατρός is ‘until he reached the halls of his father’. ἀμφὶ δέ με χλαῖνάν τε χιτῶνά τε εἵματα ἕσσεν is ‘and he put clothes about me, a cloak and a tunic’: ἀμφὶ … ἕσσεν is tmesis for ἀμφιέννυμι ‘put about’, and the line is a stock line, here with a man as its subject (the king’s son), so the English has ‘he’. The raised dot after πατρός falls inside this unit, which is kept whole so that ἕσσεν has its subject, the king’s son, in view. Odysseus has not finished: the speech goes on into the next part, so no closing quotation mark is set here.
